title: Latin America’s new imaginaries – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: A short ECFR podcast episode description (recorded July 31st 2026) in which Mark Leonard, Adriana Abdenur and former Mexican foreign minister Jorge Castañeda discuss why China's role varies sharply across Latin America — Mexico and Central America constrained by US economic ties, Brazil drawing on a long strategic-autonomy tradition and treating China as both market and source of development ideas. This is a listing blurb, not an argument, so the extractable signal is limited to the framing of the region's US-China balancing question.

themes.theme: China's uneven footprint in Latin America

insights.claim: China's role differs materially by sub-region within Latin America, with Mexico and much of Central America remaining deeply constrained in their China options by their economic ties to the United States.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Treat 'Latin America' as at least two distinct China-exposure blocs when sizing supply-chain or nearshoring positions — Mexican policy space is structurally narrower.
insights.quote: arguing that Mexico and much of Central America remain deeply constrained by their economic ties to the US
insights.locator: Jorge explains why China’s role is varied

insights.claim: Brazilian policymakers engage with China not only as an economic partner but as a source of ideas on development, technology and global governance, drawing on Brazil's long tradition of strategic autonomy.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
entities: Global Fund for a New Economy
insights.so_what: Brazil's China relationship is ideational as well as commercial, implying more durable alignment on technology and governance standards than trade flows alone suggest.
insights.quote: describing how policymakers engage with China as both an economic partner and a source of ideas on development, technology and global governance

insights.claim: The episode frames the open question as whether Latin American countries can balance both powers at all, and whether China functions as a model, a market or simply another partner in a multipolar world.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: A useful three-way classification for reading Latin American policy moves: model-following, market-seeking, or transactional hedging imply very different durability.
insights.quote: Is China a model, a market or simply another partner in a multipolar world?
insights.locator: Together, Mark, Adriana and Jorge explore

insights.claim: Intensifying US-China competition is reshaping Latin America's choices in what the participants characterise as an increasingly coercive geopolitical environment, putting strategic autonomy itself under pressure.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
insights.so_what: Non-alignment as a Latin American default is being tested; coercion episodes (tariffs, sanctions, tech restrictions) are the events to watch for forced alignment.
insights.quote: And what does strategic autonomy look like in an increasingly coercive geopolitical environment?
insights.locator: Can Latin American countries balance relations
